flashcards.q: What are the three types of XSS and how do they differ in where the payload lives?
flashcards.a: Stored XSS: payload persisted server-side, hits every viewer (highest severity). Reflected XSS: payload round-trips through a single request, needs a victim to click a crafted link. DOM-based XSS: never touches the server, purely client-side sink (e.g. innerHTML = location.hash).

flashcards.q: Does httpOnly on a session cookie prevent XSS?
flashcards.a: No -- it stops a successful XSS payload from exfiltrating the raw cookie value via JS, but a live XSS payload can still make authenticated requests AS the user while executing, since the browser still auto-attaches the cookie. It bounds the blast radius, doesn't prevent the incident.

flashcards.q: How does a nonce-based CSP defend against XSS even after a successful injection?
flashcards.a: A strict CSP (script-src 'self' 'nonce-X') makes the browser refuse to execute any script lacking the correct per-response random nonce. An attacker's injected <script> tag has no way to know that nonce, so even though it's present in the DOM, the browser won't execute it.

flashcards.q: What is CSRF's core mechanism, and what are the two main defenses?
flashcards.a: Browsers auto-attach a site's cookies to ANY request to that site regardless of which page initiated it, letting an attacker's page trigger state-changing requests on a logged-in victim's behalf. Defenses: SameSite=Lax/Strict cookies (Chromium default since 2020) + an explicit unpredictable anti-CSRF token, since SameSite alone has documented bypasses.

flashcards.q: What does CORS actually protect, and what is the most common misunderstanding about it?
flashcards.a: CORS is a browser-enforced relaxation of the same-origin policy governing whether a CALLING PAGE'S JavaScript may READ a cross-origin response. It does NOT block the request from reaching the server -- a direct curl/server-to-server request ignores CORS entirely. Common misunderstanding: treating CORS as a server-hardening/authentication control.

flashcards.q: What specific CORS misconfiguration is actually dangerous?
flashcards.a: Reflecting the request's Origin header back unconditionally COMBINED WITH Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true -- this lets any origin make an authenticated, cookie-carrying cross-origin request via the victim's browser and successfully READ the response containing private data.

flashcards.q: What is clickjacking's mechanism and fix?
flashcards.a: An attacker overlays an invisible iframe of the real, authenticated site over a decoy UI, so the victim's click actually hits the real site's button underneath. Fix: X-Frame-Options: DENY/SAMEORIGIN, or the modern CSP frame-ancestors directive which supersedes it.

flashcards.q: What is the canonical real-world SSRF case and its attack chain?
flashcards.a: The 2019 Capital One breach: a misconfigured WAF on EC2 had an SSRF vulnerability; the attacker made it fetch the unauthenticated cloud metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254), retrieved live IAM credentials, and used them to exfiltrate 100M+ customer records from S3. Chain: SSRF -> metadata credential theft -> data exfiltration, one crafted request.

flashcards.q: What does IMDSv2 add over IMDSv1, and what does it NOT fix?
flashcards.a: IMDSv2 requires a session-token handshake (PUT for a token, then GET with it) that a basic single-GET SSRF exploit can't easily replicate, closing the simplest SSRF-to-metadata-credential-theft chain. It does NOT fix SSRF generally -- the same vulnerability can still reach other internal infrastructure unaffected by IMDS version.

flashcards.q: Why is blocklisting SSRF targets fragile compared to allowlisting?
flashcards.a: Blocklists must anticipate every alternate representation: decimal/octal IP encodings, redirect chains that pass validation then redirect to a blocked address, and DNS rebinding (hostname resolves safely at check-time, maliciously at request-time). An allowlist of specific permitted hosts sidesteps all of this.

flashcards.q: What happened to SSRF's category status in the OWASP Top 10 2025 refresh?
flashcards.a: SSRF was folded back into the broader Broken Access Control category (A01:2025) rather than standing alone as it did in 2021 (A10:2021), though the underlying vulnerability and its cloud-specific severity haven't changed.
